This is an MCP server for Datadog (a software observability platform). Consult Datadog docs if you're unsure about how something works in the platform. Docs for this MCP server can be found at https://docs.datadoghq.com/bits_ai/mcp_server/setup/ This server ships skill guides containing domain-specific guidance, workflows, and best practices that are not visible in tool names or schemas. Before invoking other tools, always perform skill discovery by running both paths in parallel: a direct load with `load_datadog_skill` using a general domain name (e.g. skill_name='datadog/traces'), and a call to `list_datadog_skills` with a fuzzy `query` based on topic keywords — load any clearly matching result from the listing along with the related skills it points to. The exception is a follow-up call in a domain whose skill you have already loaded or confirmed absent this session. If nothing clearly fits, do not load a skill — proceed with the tool descriptions. ## claude.ai entire-prod-us
Entire MCP — an investigation surface over Entire's engineering data: repos and their analytics, git history (commits, files, trees, refs, diffs), the AI checkpoints and sessions behind the code (with transcripts and token accounting), trails (PR-like change proposals), and code search. Reads are curated `*_entire` tools; a small write/ops group covers trail/review/runner/dispatch mutations.

Workflow: when you only have a repo name, path, or URL, call resolve_entire_repo first, then pass the repo it returns to repo-scoped tools. Prefer the aggregation tools (get_entire_repo_overview, get_entire_my_activity) over hand-rolling stats from raw listings.

Querying conventions (shared by every tool):
- Addressing: name a repo by a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, git/<owner>/<repo>) or a repo ULID. Repo ULIDs are REGION-SCOPED — the same repo has a different ULID per region, so never carry a ULID across regions or sessions; if a tool rejects one, re-resolve with resolve_entire_repo.
- Pagination: every list takes an opaque cursor and returns next_cursor when more remains — exhaust the pages before concluding "that's all".
- Time: since/until are ISO 8601 / RFC3339 bounds; where offered, timeframe is a relative window (last-month, last-3-months, last-6-months).
- Size: reads that can be large (files, diffs, transcripts) honor max_tokens and return next_cursor to continue — raise max_tokens or page rather than assuming truncation is the whole story.

Pitfalls:
- sessions[].tokenUsage on a checkpoint is a PER-CHECKPOINT delta, not a session total — sum across a session's checkpoints, or use get_entire_session for the authoritative total.
- list_entire_checkpoints silently truncates older history; for a branch's COMPLETE checkpoint membership, paginate list_entire_commits and collect the per-commit checkpoint IDs.

Skills: before deep work in a domain, load the matching skill (list_entire_skills / load_entire_skill) — entire/checkpoints-and-sessions and entire/token-analysis before token accounting, … [truncated]

## claude.ai incident.io
The incident.io MCP server lets you query and manage incidents, alerts, escalations, schedules, follow-ups, catalog data, and telemetry.

If another connected MCP server exposes an incident_pin tool (alongside incident_list, incident_show, etc.), that is the incident.io desktop server — prefer it for every incident.io action. It is a superset of this one: it proxies these same tools and adds local-only capabilities (the user's pinned incident, locally-cached investigations, opening links). Don't split a task across both servers — in particular, an ask / ask_incident / ask_telemetry session_id from this server is not valid on the desktop server, so keep each conversation on whichever server it started on.

Before you start:
- Read config://organisation to discover severity IDs, custom field IDs, role IDs, and other values you'll need for filtering and grouping.
- Read playbook://analysis before doing any analytical or reporting work — it indexes all analysis playbooks and helps you pick the right one for the user's question. Then call analysis_start to download the playbook workspace.

Tool selection:
- analysis_start — call this BEFORE doing any analytical or reporting work (e.g. "analyse my incidents", "prepare for the review", "how are we doing?"). It downloads playbooks with step-by-step methodology, org config, and a branded HTML report template. Follow the playbook stages rather than ad-hoc querying — it produces much better analysis.
- stats tools (incident_stats, alert_stats, escalation_stats, follow_up_stats) — for counts, trends, and workload breakdowns across many records. Start here for analytical questions.
- list tools (incident_list, alert_list, etc.) — to browse or search individual records. Use the include parameter on incident_list to enrich results with roles or custom fields without calling incident_show for each one.
- show tools (incident_show, alert_show, etc.) — for full detail on a specific record. For investigation or root cause analysis, always request include: ["investigation", "postmor… [truncated]

Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. - code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. - loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. {"id":"ENT-1535","title":"entire-search: the ENT-1492 DLQ doesn't prevent the stall — a poison ref event still pins the ack floor for ~18h before it dead-letters","description":"## Summary

<issue id="96688401-2b2d-48dd-8a77-a4400bd1bb45" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1492/entire-search-exhausted-ref-events-are-termed-which-does-not-settle">ENT-1492</issue> shipped the DLQ + `Ack()` fix so exhausted ref events stop leaking as unsettled `Term()`s. That fixed the *permanent* wedge and the silent data loss. It did **not** fix the stall that pages us.

On 2026-08-06 the same P1 fired again on `eks-prod-us-east-2`: one poison ref event pinned the `search-indexer-refs` ack floor for ~9h and search results went stale until a human manually deleted the message from the stream. The DLQ was still empty at the time of the page, because the retry ladder had not yet reached `MaxDeliver=7`.

**The gap:** the monitor fires at 50m of no floor movement, but the earliest the DLQ path can possibly run is **\~17h45m** after first delivery. Between those two points the consumer is stalled and nothing in the system recovers it. Dead-lettering is the right terminal behaviour; it is just far too late to be the stall remedy.

## Timeline (2026-08-06, all times UTC)

| Time | Event |
| -- | -- |
| 02:34:05 | seq **2,774,437** published — `refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1` update on repo `01KWHDFJ0C575CRVF18DPVSQW0` |
| ~04:11 | ack floor stops advancing at seq **2,774,436** |
| 04:13 | first investigation on this repo/message (earlier thread) — not resolved |
| 12:23 | P1 page: `search-indexer ack floor stalled (throughput collapse)` |
| 12:23 | floor `2,774,436` / delivered `2,791,157` — ~16,700-seq gap, `num_ack_pending: 6`; `repo_refs_dlq_v1` = **0 messages** |
| 13:22 | floor unchanged, delivered `2,792,806` — gap now ~18,370, `num_ack_pending: 2`; DLQ still **0 messages** |
| 13:28 | operator removes seq 2,774,436 via `./bin/nats-admin … stream rmm repo_refs_v1 2774436 -f` |
| ~13:31 | operator removes seq **2,774,437**, the actual blocker |
| 13:32 | floor jumps to **2,792,129**, delivered `2,793,074`, outstanding acks 1 — consumer caught up |

## Why the DLQ can't arrive in time

Live consumer config, read at 13:32Z:

```
Maximum Deliveries: 7
           Ack Wait: 5m0s
            Backoff: 5m0s, 10m0s, 30m0s, 1h0m0s, 4h0m0s, 12h0m0s
```

Seven deliveries means six backoff waits: `5m + 10m + 30m + 1h + 4h + 12h` = **17h45m** before the terminal branch — the one <issue id="96688401-2b2d-48dd-8a77-a4400bd1bb45" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1492/entire-search-exhausted-ref-events-are-termed-which-does-not-settle">ENT-1492</issue> changed to dead-letter and `Ack()` — is even reached. For a message first delivered at 02:34Z that is roughly 20:19Z. The page fired at 12:23Z and a human intervened at 13:28Z, both many hours ahead of it.

So the empty DLQ observed at 12:23Z and 13:22Z is *expected behaviour*, not evidence the <issue id="96688401-2b2d-48dd-8a77-a4400bd1bb45" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1492/entire-search-exhausted-ref-events-are-termed-which-does-not-settle">ENT-1492</issue> fix is broken or undeployed. The runbook's step 2 currently reads an empty DLQ as "the DLQ capture path itself is failing" and points at `settle:dlq_publish_failed` / `settle:dlq_ack_failed`; during the first ~18h that inference is wrong and sends the responder down a dead end.

**Not verified:** the observed retry log lines for this repo (03:09:35, 03:10:53, 03:18:23, 03:53:53, 05:49:24Z) don't line up cleanly with the configured ladder — the first two are ~78s apart. Either several distinct events for that repo are interleaved in those lines, or the effective backoff isn't the configured one. Worth confirming before sizing any ladder change, since the whole argument above rests on the ladder's real timing.

## Manual remediation now works, but it is undocumented and lossy

<issue id="96688401-2b2d-48dd-8a77-a4400bd1bb45" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1492/entire-search-exhausted-ref-events-are-termed-which-does-not-settle">ENT-1492</issue> recorded that all four operator escape hatches were walled off — in particular `stream rmm` on `repo_refs_v1` failed with a permissions violation. The `nats-admin` break-glass launcher added since (`incidents@184d072`) carries a MUTATING `internal-tls` identity and **does** succeed:

```
./bin/nats-admin --context eks-prod-us-east-2-admin -- stream rmm repo_refs_v1 2774436 -f
nats-admin: eks-prod-us-east-2-admin/mirror-worker -> pod/nats-admin-20260806-152806-16072 (MUTATING identity: internal-tls)
```

Two problems with that being the de-facto remedy:

* **It destroys the event with no record.** Seq 2,774,437 was deleted from the stream, never indexed, and never captured to `repo_refs_dlq_v1`. The only surviving trace of it is a paste in a Slack thread. This is exactly the data loss <issue id="96688401-2b2d-48dd-8a77-a4400bd1bb45" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1492/entire-search-exhausted-ref-events-are-termed-which-does-not-settle">ENT-1492</issue> set out to end, reintroduced through the break-glass path.
* **There is no runbook for it.** `runbooks/` in the incidents repo covers `eks-access.md` only, and the monitor text still describes the pre-`nats-admin` world. The operator also deleted seq 2,774,436 first — harmless, since that sequence *is* the settled floor boundary and was already acked, but it's a natural misreading of `consumer info` output that a runbook should head off.

## Proposed work

1. **Give the stall a remedy that fits inside the page window.** Options, roughly in order of preference — pick one deliberately rather than doing all three:
   * Shorten the ladder for terminal-eligible failures so `MaxDeliver` is reached in well under an hour, keeping the long ladder only for failure classes that genuinely benefit from a 12h wait (e.g. entiredb outages).
   * Add a floor-age circuit breaker: if the floor hasn't advanced in N minutes and one message is responsible, dead-letter that message immediately regardless of attempt count.
   * Related prior art: <issue id="6724c280-8edf-4b58-9bcc-37c4e8ad7adc" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1038/semantic-search-consumer-level-circuit-breaker-pause-nats-consumption">ENT-1038</issue> (consumer-level circuit breaker on systemic entiredb outage) covers the outage-shaped case, not the single-poison-message case here.
2. **Make break-glass non-lossy.** A `nats-admin`-side path (or a small tool) that copies the message to `repo_refs_dlq_v1` *before* deleting it from `repo_refs_v1`, so manual unblocking keeps the same record the automated path produces.
3. **Write the runbook** — `runbooks/nats-poison-ref-event.md`: read `consumer info`, the blocker is `floor + 1` (not the floor), inspect it with `natsctl stream get`, capture-then-delete with `nats-admin`, verify the floor advances. Do not restart the indexer (<issue id="a3e7698e-f13e-49c7-9d2e-d4a1aea58a09" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1460/entire-search-indexer-never-drains-in-flight-nats-messages-on-sigterm">ENT-1460</issue>).
4. **Fix the monitor's step 2 text** so an empty DLQ inside the first ~18h reads as "ladder not exhausted yet", not "DLQ capture is failing".
5. **Root-cause the poison message itself.** Repo `01KWHDFJ0C575CRVF18DPVSQW0`'s `refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1` updates have now stalled this consumer at least twice in one day. The working hypothesis from the thread is checkpoint metadata that never hydrates in entiredb for that repo — **this was never independently confirmed against entiredb** and should be, since a fix here prevents the page rather than just shortening it. Compare with <issue id="97e263b0-2b6a-46a2-8630-1b6df08bc25e" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1479/entire-search-refsclaims-coordination-refs-are-indexed-as-content-pins">ENT-1479</issue>, which found a different poison class (`refs/claims/*` indexed as content).

## Done when

* A single poison ref event can no longer hold the ack floor past the monitor's own alerting window without an automated remedy kicking in
* Manual break-glass removal captures the message to `repo_refs_dlq_v1` before deleting it
* `runbooks/nats-poison-ref-event.md` exists and the monitor text points at it
* The monitor no longer tells responders an empty DLQ means DLQ capture is broken
* The reason `refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1` fails indexing for repo `01KWHDFJ0C575CRVF18DPVSQW0` is confirmed against entiredb and either fixed or split into its own ticket

That fixed the *permanent* wedge and the silent data loss. It did **not** fix the stall that pages us.

On 2026-08-06 the same P1 fired again on `eks-prod-us-east-2`: one poison ref event pinned the `search-indexer-refs` ack floor for ~9h and search results went stale until a human manually deleted the message from the stream. The DLQ was still empty at the time of the page, because the retry ladder had not yet reached `MaxDeliver=7`.

**The gap:** the monitor fires at 50m of no floor movement, but the earliest the DLQ path can possibly run is **\~17h45m** after first delivery. Between those two points the consumer is stalled and nothing in the system recovers it. Dead-lettering is the right terminal behaviour; it is just far too late to be the stall remedy.

## Timeline (2026-08-06, all times UTC)

| Time | Event |
| -- | -- |
| 02:34:05 | seq **2,774,437** published — `refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1` update on repo `01KWHDFJ0C575CRVF18DPVSQW0` |
| ~04:11 | ack floor stops advancing at seq **2,774,436** |
| 04:13 | first investigation on this repo/message (earlier thread) — not resolved |
| 12:23 | P1 page: `search-indexer ack floor stalled (throughput collapse)` |
| 12:23 | floor `2,774,436` / delivered `2,791,157` — ~16,700-seq gap, `num_ack_pending: 6`; `repo_refs_dlq_v1` = **0 messages** |
| 13:22 | floor unchanged, delivered `2,792,806` — gap now ~18,370, `num_ack_pending: 2`; DLQ still **0 messages** |
| 13:28 | operator removes seq 2,774,436 via `./bin/nats-admin … stream rmm repo_refs_v1 2774436 -f` |
| ~13:31 | operator removes seq **2,774,437**, the actual blocker |
| 13:32 | floor jumps to **2,792,129**, delivered `2,793,074`, outstanding acks 1 — consumer caught up |

## Why the DLQ can't arrive in time

Live consumer config, read at 13:32Z:

```
Maximum Deliveries: 7
           Ack Wait: 5m0s
            Backoff: 5m0s, 10m0s, 30m0s, 1h0m0s, 4h0m0s, 12h0m0s
```

Seven deliveries means six backoff waits: `5m + 10m + 30m + 1h + 4h + 12h` = **17h45m** before the terminal branch — the one <issue id="96688401-2b2d-48dd-8a77-a4400bd1bb45" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1492/entire-search-exhausted-ref-events-are-termed-which-does-not-settle">ENT-1492</issue> changed to dead-letter and `Ack()` — is even reached. For a message first delivered at 02:34Z that is roughly 20:19Z. The page fired at 12:23Z and a human intervened at 13:28Z, both many hours ahead of it.

So the empty DLQ observed at 12:23Z and 13:22Z is *expected behaviour*, not evidence the <issue id="96688401-2b2d-48dd-8a77-a4400bd1bb45" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1492/entire-search-exhausted-ref-events-are-termed-which-does-not-settle">ENT-1492</issue> fix is broken or undeployed. The runbook's step 2 currently reads an empty DLQ as "the DLQ capture path itself is failing" and points at `settle:dlq_publish_failed` / `settle:dlq_ack_failed`; during the first ~18h that inference is wrong and sends the responder down a dead end.

**Not verified:** the observed retry log lines for this repo (03:09:35, 03:10:53, 03:18:23, 03:53:53, 05:49:24Z) don't line up cleanly with the configured ladder — the first two are ~78s apart. Either several distinct events for that repo are interleaved in those lines, or the effective backoff isn't the configured one. Worth confirming before sizing any ladder change, since the whole argument above rests on the ladder's real timing.

## Manual remediation now works, but it is undocumented and lossy

<issue id="96688401-2b2d-48dd-8a77-a4400bd1bb45" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1492/entire-search-exhausted-ref-events-are-termed-which-does-not-settle">ENT-1492</issue> recorded that all four operator escape hatches were walled off — in particular `stream rmm` on `repo_refs_v1` failed with a permissions violation. The `nats-admin` break-glass launcher added since (`incidents@184d072`) carries a MUTATING `internal-tls` identity and **does** succeed:

```
nats-admin: eks-prod-us-east-2-admin/mirror-worker -> pod/nats-admin-20260806-152806-16072 (MUTATING identity: internal-tls)
```

Two problems with that being the de-facto remedy:

* **It destroys the event with no record.** Seq 2,774,437 was deleted from the stream, never indexed, and never captured to `repo_refs_dlq_v1`. The only surviving trace of it is a paste in a Slack thread. This is exactly the data loss <issue id="96688401-2b2d-48dd-8a77-a4400bd1bb45" href="https://linear.app/entirehq/issue/ENT-1492/entire-search-exhausted-ref-events-are-termed-which-does-not-settle">ENT-1492</issue> set out to end, reintroduced through the break-glass path.
* **There is no runbook for it.** `runbooks/` in the incidents repo covers `eks-access.md` only, and the monitor text still describes the pre-`nats-admin` world. 1	// Package jsconsumer is the durable JetStream pull-consumer scaffold shared by
2	// Entire's decode-and-dispatch consumers. Each of those used to hand-roll the
3	// same lifecycle: jetstream.New → CreateOrUpdateConsumer (durable, explicit
4	// ack, bounded ack-wait, bounded MaxDeliver, filter subject) → Consume → stop
5	// on context cancel; and the same per-message prologue: open a consumer span
6	// (re-parented across the NATS hop), decode the payload, and Term on a decode
7	// error.
8	//
9	// This package owns exactly that scaffold and nothing else. Each consumer
10	// keeps its OWN event type, business dispatch, metrics, and log lines — Start
11	// takes the consumer's message callback, and Process invokes the consumer's
12	// handle with the decoded event and the live span. The handler owns the
13	// message's terminal disposition (Ack/Nak/Term); Process never touches a
14	// message that decoded.
15	//
16	// Lifted from entire-api's internal/jsconsumer (COR-929), folding in the
17	// module's shutdown classification ([nuts.IsShutdownFetchErr] gates the
18	// consume-error log so a drain during rollout isn't reported as a fault,
19	// COR-923) and an optional [natsmsg.KeepInProgress] heartbeat for consumers
20	// whose handlers legitimately outrun AckWait.
21	package jsconsumer
22	
23	import (
24		"context"
25		"errors"
26		"fmt"
27		"log/slog"
28		"sync"
29		"time"
30	
31		"github.com/nats-io/nats.go"
32		"github.com/nats-io/nats.go/jetstream"
33		"go.opentelemetry.io/otel"
34		"go.opentelemetry.io/otel/codes"
35		"go.opentelemetry.io/otel/trace"
36	
37		"github.com/entireio/go-nuts"
38		"github.com/entireio/go-nuts/natsmsg"
39	)
40	
41	const (
42		// DefaultAckWait is how long JetStream waits for an ack before redelivery
43		// when Config.AckWait is zero — comfortably longer than an RPC round-trip
44		// plus a DB upsert, short enough that a stuck message redelivers promptly.
45		DefaultAckWait = 30 * time.Second
46		// DefaultMaxDeliver caps redelivery before JetStream stops redelivering a
47		// message when Config.MaxDeliver is zero.
48		DefaultMaxDeliver = 8
49	)
50	
51	// Config describes the durable consumer to create and how to trace/log it. The
52	// filter is given as either FilterSubject (single) or FilterSubjects (multi),
53	// mirroring jetstream.ConsumerConfig, so a migrated consumer preserves its
54	// existing on-server filter form exactly.
55	type Config struct {
56		Stream         string        // JetStream stream to bind (must already exist)
57		Durable        string        // durable consumer name, stable across restarts
58		FilterSubject  string        // set this OR FilterSubjects
59		FilterSubjects []string      // set this OR FilterSubject
60		AckWait        time.Duration // 0 → DefaultAckWait (see EffectiveAckWait)
61		MaxDeliver     int           // 0 → DefaultMaxDeliver (see EffectiveMaxDeliver)
62		SpanName       string        // per-message consumer span name (e.g. "repolifecycle.consume")
63		Name           string        // short consumer name, used as the log prefix
64	
65		// InactiveThreshold mirrors jetstream.ConsumerConfig.InactiveThreshold:
66		// how long the durable may go without an active subscription before the
67		// server deletes it; zero means never (the JetStream default for
68		// durables). Consumers on interest-retention streams set this so a
69		// decommissioned durable stops pinning every message it would have
70		// received, instead of holding them until the stream's MaxAge.
71		InactiveThreshold time.Duration
72	
73		// MaxAckPending mirrors jetstream.ConsumerConfig.MaxAckPending: the
74		// server-side cap on deliveries outstanding un-acked across ALL replicas
75		// sharing the durable; zero uses the server default (1000). Distinct
76		// from MaxMessages below, which caps only this process's client-side
77		// buffer.
78		MaxAckPending int
79	
80		// Tracer opens the per-message consumer span; nil uses the global OTel
81		// tracer provider.
82		Tracer trace.Tracer
83		// Logger receives the scaffold's own log lines (decode-term warnings,
84		// consume errors); nil uses slog.Default.
85		Logger *slog.Logger
86	
87		// KeepInProgress runs a natsmsg.KeepInProgress heartbeat while handle
88		// executes, for handlers that legitimately outrun AckWait. The extension
89		// is capped, so a wedged handler still redelivers — see
90		// natsmsg.KeepInProgress. The heartbeat stops when handle returns; a tick
91		// racing the handler's own terminal Ack/Nak/Term is a client-side no-op
92		// (nats.go marks the message disposed locally) that halts the heartbeat.
93		//
94		// Setting this forces the prefetch to one message (see MaxMessages): the
95		// heartbeat extends only the delivery the handler holds, so anything
96		// buffered behind a long handler would exhaust its AckWait unextended.
97		KeepInProgress bool
98	
99		// MaxMessages caps how many deliveries the consume loop buffers
100		// client-side (jetstream.PullMaxMessages); 0 uses the nats.go default
101		// (500). AckWait runs from server delivery into that buffer, not from
102		// callback dispatch, and callbacks run serially — so a consumer whose
103		// handler can approach AckWait should keep this small or queued
104		// deliveries expire and redeliver concurrently to other replicas.
105		// KeepInProgress forces it to 1; setting both to conflicting values is a
106		// Start error.
107		MaxMessages int
108	}
109	
110	// EffectiveAckWait is the AckWait actually applied to the JetStream consumer:
111	// Config.AckWait, or DefaultAckWait when zero. Use it — not the raw field —
112	// anywhere the real value matters, e.g. wiring a natsmsg.KeepInProgress
113	// heartbeat by hand (a zero ackWait there is a no-op).
114	func (c Config) EffectiveAckWait() time.Duration {
115		if c.AckWait == 0 {
116			return DefaultAckWait
117		}
118		return c.AckWait
119	}
120	
121	// EffectiveMaxDeliver is the MaxDeliver actually applied to the JetStream
122	// consumer: Config.MaxDeliver, or DefaultMaxDeliver when zero. Use it — not
123	// the raw field — when building a backoff.Policy for this consumer's
124	// messages: the two packages read zero differently (here it means "default
125	// to DefaultMaxDeliver"; on the policy it means unlimited redeliveries, the
126	// jetstream.ConsumerConfig semantics), so passing a zero Config.MaxDeliver
127	// through verbatim would make TermOnExhaustion never fire on the broker's
128	// real final delivery and orphan work-queue messages (COR-762).
129	func (c Config) EffectiveMaxDeliver() int {
130		if c.MaxDeliver == 0 {
131			return DefaultMaxDeliver
132		}
133		return c.MaxDeliver
134	}
135	
136	// validate rejects the configuration errors no retry can fix; shared by
137	// [Start] (one-shot) and [Run] (supervised, which must fail fast on these
138	// rather than retry them forever).
139	func (c Config) validate(nc *nats.Conn, onMsg func(jetstream.Msg)) error {
140		if c.KeepInProgress && c.MaxMessages > 1 {
141			return fmt.Errorf("jsconsumer(%s): KeepInProgress requires MaxMessages <= 1: the heartbeat extends only the in-flight delivery, so %d buffered messages would exhaust AckWait behind a long handler", c.Name, c.MaxMessages)
142		}
143		if c.Stream == "" {
144			return fmt.Errorf("jsconsumer(%s): Stream is required", c.Name)
145		}
146		if c.Durable == "" {
147			// CreateOrUpdateConsumer accepts an empty durable and silently makes
148			// an ephemeral, server-named consumer — losing the stable
149			// resume-across-restarts behavior this scaffold promises.
150			return fmt.Errorf("jsconsumer(%s): Durable is required", c.Name)
151		}
152		if onMsg == nil {
153			return fmt.Errorf("jsconsumer(%s): onMsg is required", c.Name)
154		}
155		if c.FilterSubject != "" && len(c.FilterSubjects) != 0 {
156			return fmt.Errorf("jsconsumer(%s): set FilterSubject or FilterSubjects, not both", c.Name)
157		}
158		for i, subject := range c.FilterSubjects {
159			if subject == "" {
160				return fmt.Errorf("jsconsumer(%s): FilterSubjects[%d] is empty", c.Name, i)
161			}
162		}
163		if c.AckWait < 0 {
164			return fmt.Errorf("jsconsumer(%s): AckWait must not be negative", c.Name)
165		}
166		if c.MaxDeliver < -1 {
167			return fmt.Errorf("jsconsumer(%s): MaxDeliver must be -1 (unlimited), 0 (default), or positive", c.Name)
168		}
169		if c.MaxMessages < 0 {
170			return fmt.Errorf("jsconsumer(%s): MaxMessages must not be negative", c.Name)
171		}
172		if c.MaxAckPending < -1 {
173			return fmt.Errorf("jsconsumer(%s): MaxAckPending must be -1 (unlimited), 0 (server default), or positive", c.Name)
174		}
175		if c.InactiveThreshold < 0 {
176			return fmt.Errorf("jsconsumer(%s): InactiveThreshold must not be negative", c.Name)
177		}
178		if nc == nil {
179			return fmt.Errorf("jsconsumer(%s): nil nats conn", c.Name)
180		}
181		return nil
182	}
183	
184	func (c Config) tracer() trace.Tracer {
185		if c.Tracer == nil {
186			return otel.Tracer("github.com/entireio/go-nuts/jsconsumer")
187		}
188		return c.Tracer
189	}
190	
191	func (c Config) logger() *slog.Logger {
192		if c.Logger == nil {
193			return slog.Default()
194		}
195		return c.Logger
196	}
197	
198	// isShutdownConsumeErr reports whether a consume error is the benign result
199	// of the connection going away during shutdown. [nuts.IsShutdownFetchErr]
200	// covers the core nats.go sentinels, but the jetstream consume loop surfaces
201	// its OWN [jetstream.ErrConnectionClosed] — a distinct value that wraps
202	// neither — so it must be matched separately or a clean rollout drain still
203	// logs a warning (the COR-923 noise this suppression exists to remove). As
204	// with the root classifier, it is only "clean" when ctx is already done; a
205	// mid-run connection loss is a genuine fault worth logging.
206	func isShutdownConsumeErr(ctx context.Context, err error) bool {
207		return nuts.IsShutdownFetchErr(ctx, err) ||
208			(ctx.Err() != nil && errors.Is(err, jetstream.ErrConnectionClosed))
209	}
210	
211	// Runner is a live consume loop. Stop halts it and is idempotent.
212	type Runner struct {
213		cc jetstream.ConsumeContext
214		// closed is cc.Closed(), captured while the subscription is live (the
215		// same channel is returned on every call, so capturing once avoids any
216		// post-Stop race) — it closes when the consume loop has fully wound
217		// down, including an in-flight handler.
218		closed <-chan struct{}
219		// watcherDone closes when Start's context-cancellation watcher exits. It is
220		// intentionally internal: callers synchronize on Stop, while tests pin that
221		// an explicit Stop does not retain a goroutine until the parent context ends.
222		watcherDone <-chan struct{}
223		stop        sync.Once
224	}
225	
226	// Stop halts the consume loop and blocks until it has fully wound down —
227	// including an in-flight handler — so a caller may tear down what handlers
228	// use (stores, publishers, the NATS connection) the moment it returns: the
229	// cancel → join → drain shutdown ordering (COR-923). Safe on a nil or
230	// never-Started Runner, idempotent, and safe for concurrent use — an
231	// explicit Stop can race the context-cancel stop armed by Start. Must not be
232	// called from inside the handler; it would deadlock waiting on itself.
233	func (r *Runner) Stop() {
234		if r == nil || r.cc == nil {
235			return
236		}
237		r.stop.Do(r.cc.Stop)
238		<-r.closed
239	}
240	
241	// Start creates/updates the durable consumer on nc and begins delivering
242	// messages to onMsg, returning a Runner that Stops when ctx is cancelled. The
243	// stream must already exist (provisioned declaratively); callers whose cells
244	// opt in per-stream gate Start behind that opt-in so a cell without the stream
245	// doesn't error at CreateOrUpdateConsumer.
246	//
247	// Consume errors are logged at Warn, except a drain/close during shutdown —
248	// both the core nats.go sentinels ([nuts.IsShutdownFetchErr]) and jetstream's
249	// own connection-closed error — which is a clean exit rather than a fault.
250	func Start(ctx context.Context, nc *nats.Conn, cfg Config, onMsg func(jetstream.Msg)) (*Runner, error) {
251		if err := cfg.validate(nc, onMsg); err != nil {
252			return nil, err
253		}
254		js, err := jetstream.New(nc)
255		if err != nil {
256			return nil, fmt.Errorf("jsconsumer(%s): jetstream.New: %w", cfg.Name, err)
257		}
258		cons, err := js.CreateOrUpdateConsumer(ctx, cfg.Stream, jetstream.ConsumerConfig{
259			Durable:           cfg.Durable,
260			AckPolicy:         jetstream.AckExplicitPolicy,
261			AckWait:           cfg.EffectiveAckWait(),
262			MaxDeliver:        cfg.EffectiveMaxDeliver(),
263			FilterSubject:     cfg.FilterSubject,
264			FilterSubjects:    cfg.FilterSubjects,
265			InactiveThreshold: cfg.InactiveThreshold,
266			MaxAckPending:     cfg.MaxAckPending,
267		})
268		if err != nil {
269			return nil, fmt.Errorf("jsconsumer(%s): create consumer %s/%s: %w", cfg.Name, cfg.Stream, cfg.Durable, err)
270		}
271		consumeOpts := []jetstream.PullConsumeOpt{jetstream.ConsumeErrHandler(func(_ jetstream.ConsumeContext, cerr error) {
272			if isShutdownConsumeErr(ctx, cerr) {
273				return
274			}
275			cfg.logger().WarnContext(ctx, cfg.Name+": consume error", slog.Any("error", cerr))
276		})}
277		switch {
278		case cfg.KeepInProgress:
279			consumeOpts = append(consumeOpts, jetstream.PullMaxMessages(1))
280		case cfg.MaxMessages > 0:
281			consumeOpts = append(consumeOpts, jetstream.PullMaxMessages(cfg.MaxMessages))
282		}
283		cc, err := cons.Consume(onMsg, consumeOpts...)
284		if err != nil {
285			return nil, fmt.Errorf("jsconsumer(%s): consume %s: %w", cfg.Name, cfg.Stream, err)
286		}
287		watcherDone := make(chan struct{})
288		r := &Runner{cc: cc, closed: cc.Closed(), watcherDone: watcherDone}
289		go func() {
290			defer close(watcherDone)
291			select {
292			case <-ctx.Done():
293				r.Stop()
294			case <-r.closed:
295			}
296		}()
297		return r, nil
298	}
299	
300	// isRetryableStartError classifies the narrow set of failures that can become
301	// healthy without changing Config or replacing nc. Everything else returns to
302	// the owner so a bad deployment cannot stay alive indefinitely with no
303	// consumer. Unknown server-side 5xx responses are retried, except known
304	// permanent JetStream configuration/account errors whose API happens to use a
305	// 5xx status.
306	func isRetryableStartError(err error) bool {
307		if errors.Is(err, jetstream.ErrStreamNotFound) ||
308			errors.Is(err, nats.ErrNoResponders) ||
309			errors.Is(err, nats.ErrTimeout) ||
310			errors.Is(err, nats.ErrDisconnected) {
311			return true
312		}
313	
314		var jsErr jetstream.JetStreamError
315		if !errors.As(err, &jsErr) || jsErr.APIError() == nil {
316			return false
317		}
318		apiErr := jsErr.APIError()
319		switch apiErr.ErrorCode { //nolint:exhaustive // unrecognized 5xx codes are deliberately retryable; all other unknown codes fail closed
320		case jetstream.JSErrCodeBadRequest,
321			jetstream.JSErrCodeConsumerCreate,
322			jetstream.JSErrCodeConsumerNameExists,
323			jetstream.JSErrCodeMaximumConsumersLimit,
324			jetstream.JSErrCodeJetStreamNotEnabledForAccount,
325			jetstream.JSErrCodeJetStreamNotEnabled,
326			jetstream.JSErrCodeConsumerAlreadyExists,
327			jetstream.JSErrCodeDuplicateFilterSubjects,
328			jetstream.JSErrCodeOverlappingFilterSubjects,
329			jetstream.JSErrCodeConsumerEmptyFilter,
330			jetstream.JSErrCodeConsumerExists:
331			return false
332		default:
333			return apiErr.Code >= 500
334		}
335	}
336	
337	// Retry envelope for [Run]'s supervision: exponential from runRetryInitial
338	// doubling to runRetryMax, reset once a consume loop survives longer than the
339	// max. Package vars (not consts) so tests can compress the schedule.
340	var (
341		runRetryInitial = time.Second
342		runRetryMax     = 30 * time.Second
343	)
344	
345	// Run supervises the consume loop [Start] builds. Where Start is one-shot —
346	// an error at consumer creation is returned, and a consume loop that closes
347	// underneath the caller (consumer deleted on the server, subscription
348	// invalidated) stays closed — Run retries both with exponential backoff
349	// (runRetryInitial doubling to runRetryMax, reset after a loop that outlives
350	// the max). In particular a stream that is not provisioned yet at boot — the
351	// declarative-provisioning race — is a retry, not a crash.
352	//
353	// Run blocks until ctx is cancelled, then joins the live loop (including an
354	// in-flight handler, see [Runner.Stop]) before returning, so it composes with
355	// the cancel → join → drain shutdown ordering as the body of a supervised
356	// goroutine:
357	//
358	//	g.Go(func(ctx context.Context) {
359	//		if err := jsconsumer.Run(ctx, nc, cfg, onMsg); err != nil {
360	//			log.Error("consumer config rejected", "error", err)
361	//		}
362	//	})
363	//
364	// Local configuration errors and permanent server responses (invalid consumer
365	// configuration, authorization/account setup) can never succeed on retry and
366	// are returned immediately. A missing declarative stream, temporary transport
367	// failure, or unknown server-side 5xx response remains supervised. A nil return
368	// means a clean, ctx-driven exit.
369	func Run(ctx context.Context, nc *nats.Conn, cfg Config, onMsg func(jetstream.Msg)) error {
370		if err := cfg.validate(nc, onMsg); err != nil {
371			return err
372		}
373		delay := runRetryInitial
374		for {
375			// Each attempt gets a child context so the cancel-watcher goroutine
376			// Start arms is released when the attempt dies, instead of one
377			// accumulating per recreate for the life of the process.
378			attemptCtx, cancelAttempt := context.WithCancel(ctx)
379			r, err := Start(attemptCtx, nc, cfg, onMsg)
380			if err != nil {
381				cancelAttempt()
382				if ctx.Err() != nil {
383					return nil //nolint:nilerr // a Start error during shutdown is a clean, ctx-driven exit, not a fault to report
384				}
385				if !isRetryableStartError(err) {
386					return err
387				}
388				cfg.logger().WarnContext(ctx, cfg.Name+": start consumer failed; retrying",
389					slog.Any("error", err), slog.Duration("retry_in", delay))
390			} else {
391				started := time.Now()
392				select {
393				case <-ctx.Done():
394					r.Stop()
395					cancelAttempt()
396					return nil
397				case <-r.closed:
398					cancelAttempt()
399					if ctx.Err() != nil {
400						return nil //nolint:nilerr // the loop closing during shutdown is the expected wind-down, not a fault
401					}
402					// A loop that ran long enough to be called healthy earns a
403					// fresh envelope; a flapping one keeps escalating.
404					if time.Since(started) >= runRetryMax {
405						delay = runRetryInitial
406					}
407					cfg.logger().WarnContext(ctx, cfg.Name+": consume loop closed; recreating",
408						slog.Duration("retry_in", delay))
409				}
410			}
411			select {
412			case <-ctx.Done():
413				return nil
414			case <-time.After(delay):
415			}
416			delay = min(delay*2, runRetryMax)
417		}
418	}
419	
420	// Process runs the per-message prologue shared by every consumer: open the
421	// consumer span (re-parented to the producer across the NATS hop), decode the
422	// payload, and on a decode error record it, log "<Name>: decode <Stream>;
423	// term", invoke onUndecodable (so the caller bumps its own drop metric with
424	// its own attributes), and Term the message — a poison payload won't decode on
425	// redelivery. On success it invokes handle with the span-enriched context, the
426	// live span (for RecordError/SetStatus on the business error paths), the
427	// message, and the decoded event; with Config.KeepInProgress set, an AckWait
428	// heartbeat runs for the duration of handle.
429	//
430	// Callers wire Process as the func they pass to Start AND the entry point
431	// their tests drive, so the decode-or-term path is exercised the same way in
432	// production and tests.
433	func Process[E any](
434		ctx context.Context,
435		msg jetstream.Msg,
436		cfg Config,
437		decode func([]byte) (E, error),
438		handle func(ctx context.Context, span trace.Span, msg jetstream.Msg, ev E),
439		onUndecodable func(ctx context.Context),
440	) {
441		ctx, span := natsmsg.StartConsumerSpan(ctx, cfg.tracer(), msg, cfg.SpanName)
442		defer span.End()
443	
444		ev, err := decode(msg.Data())
445		if err != nil {
446			span.RecordError(err)
447			span.SetStatus(codes.Error, "decode")
448			cfg.logger().WarnContext(ctx, cfg.Name+": decode "+cfg.Stream+"; term",
449				slog.Any("error", err), slog.String("subject", msg.Subject()))
450			if onUndecodable != nil {
451				onUndecodable(ctx)
452			}
453			if termErr := msg.Term(); termErr != nil {
454				cfg.logger().WarnContext(ctx, cfg.Name+": term failed", slog.Any("error", termErr))
455			}
456			return
457		}
458		if cfg.KeepInProgress {
459			stop := natsmsg.KeepInProgress(msg.InProgress, cfg.EffectiveAckWait())
460			defer stop()
461		}
462		handle(ctx, span, msg, ev)
463	}

1	// Package backoff is the redelivery policy for transiently-failed JetStream
2	// deliveries: a NakWithDelay envelope — flat by default, optionally growing
3	// multiplicatively per delivery — bounded by MaxDeliver, with an optional
4	// Term on the final delivery.
5	//
6	// The policy owns disposition and delay calculation only, and nothing wider:
7	// dead-letter capture, domain metrics/logging, and the decision of which
8	// failures are transient stay with the caller. It drives the modern
9	// [jetstream.Msg] API (NakOrTerm, NumDelivered, IsFinalDelivery).
10	//
11	// Delay calculation ([Policy.DelayFor]) is independent of message disposition:
12	// it is a pure function of the delivery count, so a caller can pin or meter the
13	// delay envelope without a message in hand.
14	//
15	// # Zero-value and unlimited semantics
16	//
17	// MaxDeliver matches [jetstream.ConsumerConfig.MaxDeliver]: a non-positive value
18	// (0 or [UnlimitedMaxDeliver]) means unlimited redeliveries, so no delivery is
19	// ever final and NakOrTerm always Naks. Note this reads zero differently from
20	// jsconsumer.Config.MaxDeliver, where 0 means "default to DefaultMaxDeliver":
21	// bridge with jsconsumer.Config.EffectiveMaxDeliver() (never the raw field), so
22	// an unset consumer MaxDeliver becomes the real default here instead of
23	// unlimited. Missing message metadata (a synthetic test message) reads as the
24	// first delivery — base NakDelay, never final — the safe default being another
25	// retry, not a Term.
26	//
27	// The Term-on-exhaustion posture is the COR-762 fix, lifted from
28	// mirror-pipeline's fanoutengine: on the final delivery a Nak is dropped
29	// silently by the broker (MaxDeliver reached), and on a WorkQueue stream the
30	// un-acked message then orphans — pinning the oldest-pending-age gauge — until
31	// StreamMaxAge finally expires it. Terming instead removes it cleanly. Streams
32	// where lingering is acceptable (a webhook stream whose max_age doubles as the
33	// retry backstop) leave TermOnExhaustion off and keep the plain Nak.
34	//
35	// Dead-letter capture stays with the caller, which should capture BEFORE
36	// disposing — gate it on [IsFinalDelivery]:
37	//
38	//	if backoff.IsFinalDelivery(msg, p.MaxDeliver) {
39	//		captureToDLQ(ctx, msg)
40	//	}
41	//	outcome, err := p.NakOrTerm(msg)
42	package backoff
43	
44	import (
45		"fmt"
46		"math"
47		"time"
48	
49		"github.com/nats-io/nats.go/jetstream"
50	)
51	
52	// UnlimitedMaxDeliver is the explicit Policy.MaxDeliver value for unlimited
53	// redeliveries (matching jetstream.ConsumerConfig.MaxDeliver, where a
54	// non-positive value disables the delivery cap). The zero value means the same
55	// thing; the named constant lets a caller say so on purpose.
56	const UnlimitedMaxDeliver = -1
57	
58	// Outcome is the disposition NakOrTerm chose, for the caller's metrics and
59	// logs.
60	type Outcome string
61	
62	const (
63		OutcomeNak  Outcome = "nak"
64		OutcomeTerm Outcome = "term"
65	)
66	
67	// Policy is the redelivery envelope a consumer applies to transient
68	// failures. MaxDeliver must match the consumer's on-server MaxDeliver — the
69	// policy detects the final delivery by comparing against it.
70	type Policy struct {
71		// NakDelay is the base delay before redelivery, and with a zero Factor
72		// the whole envelope: flat suits failures expected to clear on their own
73		// timetable, with MaxDeliver bounding the total.
74		NakDelay time.Duration
75		// Factor is the optional multiplicative growth per prior delivery: the
76		// Nth delivery naks with NakDelay × Factor^(N-1), capped at MaxDelay.
77		// Values ≤ 1 (including the zero value) keep the flat envelope. Growing
78		// envelopes suit failures that get cheaper to wait out than to retry —
79		// a downstream in a crash loop, a rate limit — where hammering on the
80		// flat cadence spends MaxDeliver too fast.
81		Factor float64
82		// MaxDelay caps the grown delay; it does nothing for a flat policy.
83		// Zero with a growing Factor leaves growth bounded only by MaxDeliver
84		// ending the redeliveries (the computed delay still saturates rather
85		// than overflowing).
86		MaxDelay time.Duration
87		// MaxDeliver is the consumer's redelivery cap
88		// (jetstream.ConsumerConfig.MaxDeliver). Non-positive (0 or
89		// UnlimitedMaxDeliver) means unlimited redeliveries — matching the
90		// jetstream field's semantics — so no delivery is ever final and NakOrTerm
91		// always Naks.
92		MaxDeliver int
93		// TermOnExhaustion makes the final delivery Term instead of Nak, so a
94		// work-queue message is removed cleanly rather than orphaning un-acked
95		// (COR-762). Callers with a DLQ capture before calling NakOrTerm.
96		TermOnExhaustion bool
97	}
98	
99	// NakOrTerm applies the policy to a transiently-failed [jetstream.Msg]
100	// delivery: NakWithDelay (see [Policy.DelayFor]) for redelivery, or — on the
101	// final delivery with TermOnExhaustion set — Term. Without TermOnExhaustion the
102	// final delivery still Naks; the broker drops the Nak at MaxDeliver and the
103	// stream's retention decides the message's fate.
104	//
105	// The returned Outcome reports which disposition was chosen, for the caller's
106	// metrics and logs. A disposition error is worth a log line but nothing more:
107	// a failed Nak redelivers via AckWait expiry anyway, and a failed Term on a
108	// work-queue stream means the message lingers exactly as it would have without
109	// the policy.
110	func (p Policy) NakOrTerm(msg jetstream.Msg) (Outcome, error) {
111		if p.TermOnExhaustion && IsFinalDelivery(msg, p.MaxDeliver) {
112			if err := msg.Term(); err != nil {
113				return OutcomeTerm, fmt.Errorf("term on final delivery: %w", err)
114			}
115			return OutcomeTerm, nil
116		}
117		if err := msg.NakWithDelay(p.DelayFor(NumDelivered(msg))); err != nil {
118			return OutcomeNak, fmt.Errorf("nak with delay: %w", err)
119		}
120		return OutcomeNak, nil
121	}
122	
123	// DelayFor reports the redelivery delay the policy applies after delivery
124	// number numDelivered (1 on first delivery): NakDelay for a flat policy,
125	// NakDelay × Factor^(numDelivered-1) capped at MaxDelay for a growing one.
126	// numDelivered ≤ 1 — including the 0 that [NumDelivered] reports when
127	// metadata is unavailable — reads as the first delivery. Exposed so a caller
128	// can log or meter the delay it is about to apply.
129	func (p Policy) DelayFor(numDelivered int) time.Duration {
130		if p.Factor <= 1 || numDelivered <= 1 {
131			return p.NakDelay
132		}
133		d := float64(p.NakDelay) * math.Pow(p.Factor, float64(numDelivered-1))
134		if p.MaxDelay > 0 && d >= float64(p.MaxDelay) {
135			return p.MaxDelay
136		}
137		if d >= float64(math.MaxInt64) {
138			// Uncapped growth outran time.Duration; saturate instead of wrapping
139			// negative (a negative NakWithDelay would redeliver immediately).
140			return math.MaxInt64
141		}
142		return time.Duration(d)
143	}
144	
145	// NumDelivered reports the JetStream delivery count of a [jetstream.Msg]
146	// (1 on first delivery), or 0 if metadata is unavailable (e.g. a synthetic test
147	// message).
148	func NumDelivered(msg jetstream.Msg) int {
149		if meta, err := msg.Metadata(); err == nil && meta != nil {
150			return int(meta.NumDelivered)
151		}
152		return 0
153	}
154	
155	// IsFinalDelivery reports whether this is the last delivery before JetStream
156	// stops redelivering (NumDelivered has reached MaxDeliver), so a transient
157	// failure here is terminal rather than another Nak-and-retry. A non-positive
158	// maxDeliver means unlimited redeliveries (the jetstream.ConsumerConfig
159	// semantics), so no delivery is final — without the guard the zero value
160	// would read every delivery as final and Term on the first failure.
161	// Unavailable metadata also reads as non-final: the safe default is another
162	// retry, not a Term.
163	func IsFinalDelivery(msg jetstream.Msg, maxDeliver int) bool {
164		if maxDeliver <= 0 {
165			return false
166		}
167		if meta, err := msg.Metadata(); err == nil && meta != nil {
168			return meta.NumDelivered >= uint64(maxDeliver)
169		}
170		return false
171	}

1	package natsmsg
2	
3	import (
4		"context"
5		"fmt"
6		"strconv"
7		"time"
8	
9		"github.com/nats-io/nats.go"
10		"github.com/nats-io/nats.go/jetstream"
11	)
12	
13	// dlqPublishTimeout bounds one dead-letter PublishMsg. The consume context has
14	// no deadline, and PublishMsg waits for the PubAck indefinitely; without a
15	// bound a NATS blip would hang the handler (and, since a one-in-flight consumer
16	// keeps a slot occupied, stall the consumer) instead of failing the capture
17	// loudly.
18	const dlqPublishTimeout = 15 * time.Second
19	
20	// DLQ provenance headers added to the captured copy so a replay tool (or a
21	// human) can see why and from where a message was dead-lettered.
22	const (
23		DLQReasonHeader    = "Nats-Dlq-Reason"
24		DLQOriginHeader    = "Nats-Dlq-Origin-Subject"
25		DLQDeliveredHeader = "Nats-Dlq-Delivered"
26		DLQStreamSeqHeader = "Nats-Dlq-Stream-Seq"
27	)
28	
29	// DLQPublisher is the publish surface DeadLetter needs — the modern
30	// [JetStream] publish primitive (satisfied by jetstream.JetStream), aliased
31	// so DeadLetter's signature reads in DLQ terms. Kept minimal so wiring can
32	// hand it the same JetStream handle the per-cell publishers already hold,
33	// and tests can stub it.
34	type DLQPublisher = JetStream
35	
36	// SubjectToken sanitizes s into a single valid NATS subject token. NATS tokens
37	// cannot contain spaces, dots, or wildcards, so every character outside
38	// [a-z0-9_-] is replaced with '_' (and letters are lowercased). Use it to turn a
39	// human-readable dead-letter reason ("bad completion payload") into a subject
40	// token ("bad_completion_payload") — publishing to an unsanitized reason would
41	// fail, so the caller would never Ack the poison off a WorkQueue.
42	func SubjectToken(s string) string {
43		// Iterate bytes, not runes: we only keep ASCII [a-z0-9_-] and map everything
44		// else (including every byte of a multi-byte rune) to '_', so a byte loop is
45		// both correct and free of a rune->byte narrowing conversion.
46		b := make([]byte, 0, len(s))
47		for i := range len(s) {
48			c := s[i]
49			switch {
50			case c >= 'a' && c <= 'z', c >= '0' && c <= '9', c == '_', c == '-':
51				b = append(b, c)
52			case c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z':
53				b = append(b, c-'A'+'a')
54			default:
55				b = append(b, '_')
56			}
57		}
58		if len(b) == 0 {
59			return "unknown"
60		}
61		return string(b)
62	}
63	
64	// DeadLetter republishes a poison message to dlqSubject, preserving its payload
65	// and headers and adding Nats-Dlq-* provenance (reason, origin subject,
66	// delivery count, stream sequence).
67	//
68	// It is the capture step a consumer runs before giving up on a message it can
69	// never process. DeadLetter copies the poison to a durable DLQ subject so it can
70	// be inspected or replayed, and the caller then removes the original from the
71	// stream — a Term on the final delivery (see backoff.Policy.TermOnExhaustion,
72	// whose doc notes callers "DLQ capture before calling NakOrTerm") or a plain
73	// Ack. Without this step a Term'd or MaxDeliver-exhausted message is discarded
74	// with no trail; DeadLetter is what makes the give-up auditable and recoverable.
75	//
76	// Returns an error if the republish fails; on error the caller MUST NOT remove
77	// the original — Nak or leave it so the poison is never dropped without a
78	// captured copy. Publishing is bounded by dlqPublishTimeout regardless of ctx's
79	// deadline.
80	func DeadLetter(ctx context.Context, pub DLQPublisher, dlqSubject string, msg jetstream.Msg, reason string) error {
81		hdr := nats.Header{}
82		for k, v := range msg.Headers() {
83			hdr[k] = append([]string(nil), v...)
84		}
85		hdr.Set(DLQReasonHeader, reason)
86		hdr.Set(DLQOriginHeader, msg.Subject())
87		if meta, err := msg.Metadata(); err == nil && meta != nil {
88			hdr.Set(DLQDeliveredHeader, strconv.FormatUint(meta.NumDelivered, 10))
89			hdr.Set(DLQStreamSeqHeader, strconv.FormatUint(meta.Sequence.Stream, 10))
90		}
91	
92		out := &nats.Msg{Subject: dlqSubject, Data: msg.Data(), Header: hdr}
93	
94		pubCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, dlqPublishTimeout)
95		defer cancel()
96		if _, err := pub.PublishMsg(pubCtx, out); err != nil {
97			return fmt.Errorf("dead-letter publish to %q: %w", dlqSubject, err)
98		}
99		return nil
100	}

14	// runEmbeddedServer starts an in-process NATS server on a random loopback port
15	// and returns its client URL. The server is shut down when the test ends.

22	// and log/signal handling are forced to test-safe values) and returns the
23	// server handle for tests that drive server-side behavior such as lame duck
24	// mode. The server is shut down when the test ends.
25	func runEmbeddedServerWith(t *testing.T, opts *natsserver.Options) *natsserver.Server {
26		t.Helper()
27		opts.Host = "127.0.0.1"
28		opts.Port = -1 // pick a free port
29		opts.NoLog = true
30		opts.NoSigs = true

43	// capturingHandler is a thread-safe slog.Handler that records log messages so
44	// tests can assert what was logged, including from background goroutines.

46		mu   sync.Mutex
47		msgs []string
48	}

51

53		h.mu.Lock()
54		h.msgs = append(h.msgs, r.Message)
55		h.mu.Unlock()
56		return nil
57	}

60	func (h *capturingHandler) WithGroup(string) slog.Handler      { return h }

1	package natsmsg
2	
3	import (
4		"context"
5		"fmt"
6		"time"
7	
8		"github.com/nats-io/nats.go"
9		"github.com/nats-io/nats.go/jetstream"
10		"go.opentelemetry.io/otel"
11		"go.opentelemetry.io/otel/attribute"
12		"go.opentelemetry.io/otel/codes"
13		"go.opentelemetry.io/otel/trace"
14	)
15	
16	// DefaultPublishTimeout bounds the wait for the broker's publish
17	// acknowledgment when a publisher's Timeout is zero. The bound matters because
18	// Entire connections reconnect forever and nats.go buffers publishes while
19	// disconnected: without it, a publisher holding an HTTP request or a message
20	// disposition would wait indefinitely behind an unreachable broker instead
21	// of failing over to its retry path (the caller's outbox, nak, or 5xx).
22	const DefaultPublishTimeout = 5 * time.Second
23	
24	// StartProducerSpan opens a producer span named name on tr, pre-tagged with
25	// the standard messaging attributes (system=nats, operation.type=publish,
26	// destination=subject) — the publish-side counterpart of [StartConsumerSpan].
27	// Extra attrs are appended. The caller owns the span and must End it, and
28	// should Inject the returned ctx into the outgoing message so the consumer can
29	// re-parent.
30	func StartProducerSpan(ctx context.Context, tr trace.Tracer, subject, name string, attrs ...attribute.KeyValue) (context.Context, trace.Span) {
31		base := append([]attribute.KeyValue{
32			attribute.String("messaging.system", "nats"),
33			attribute.String("messaging.operation.type", "publish"),
34			attribute.String("messaging.destination.name", subject),
35		}, attrs...)
36		return tr.Start(ctx, name, trace.WithSpanKind(trace.SpanKindProducer), trace.WithAttributes(base...)) //nolint:spancheck // the caller owns the span and Ends it
37	}
38	
39	// JetStream is the slice of the modern [jetstream.JetStream] API the
40	// [Publisher] drives — the ctx-native PublishMsg. jetstream.JetStream
41	// satisfies it; a test stubs the one method instead of faking the full
42	// interface. [DLQPublisher] is an alias of it: dead-lettering and publishing
43	// share the identical publish surface, so a caller can hand both the one
44	// JetStream handle it already holds.
45	type JetStream interface {
46		PublishMsg(ctx context.Context, msg *nats.Msg, opts ...jetstream.PublishOpt) (*jetstream.PubAck, error)
47	}
48	
49	// Publisher is the JetStream publish core shared by Entire's producers: a
50	// producer span, W3C trace-context injection, Nats-Msg-Id dedup, and a
51	// bounded wait for the broker's ack. Every service had grown its own copy of
52	// exactly this prologue around PublishMsg; Publisher owns the prologue and
53	// nothing else — subject construction, payload encoding, domain
54	// metrics/logging, and the response to a failed publish (outbox retry, nak,
55	// HTTP 5xx) stay with the caller.
56	type Publisher struct {
57		// JS is the JetStream publish surface (satisfied by jetstream.JetStream).
58		JS JetStream
59		// Tracer opens the producer span; nil uses the global OTel tracer
60		// provider.
61		Tracer trace.Tracer
62		// Timeout bounds the wait for the broker's PubAck; 0 uses
63		// DefaultPublishTimeout. It derives from the caller's ctx, so an
64		// already-cancelled ctx still fails fast.
65		Timeout time.Duration
66		// Operation is the caller-selected producer span name (e.g.
67		// "repo.ops.publish"); empty falls back to "publish <subject>". It names the
68		// span only — the messaging operation is recorded as the standard
69		// messaging.operation.type=publish attribute, per OTel semantic conventions,
70		// which reserve messaging.operation.name for the system-specific operation
71		// (send/ack/nack), not an application span name.
72		Operation string
73	}
74	
75	// Publish sends msg and waits — bounded by Timeout — for the broker's ack,
76	// wrapped in a producer span named by Operation (or "publish <subject>" when
77	// unset). A non-empty msgID is set as the Nats-Msg-Id header, the broker-side
78	// dedup key within the stream's duplicate window; empty leaves any Nats-Msg-Id
79	// already on msg untouched. Trace context from ctx is injected into msg's
80	// headers (msg is mutated) so the consumer span re-parents across the hop.
81	//
82	// attrs are the caller's domain span attributes (placement, job identity, …) —
83	// appended to the standard messaging.* set on the producer span. They stay
84	// caller-owned: the shared package does not know them, but records them on the
85	// span it owns so a migrated caller keeps its existing producer-span tags.
86	//
87	// The returned PubAck reports where the message landed and whether the
88	// broker deduplicated it (PubAck.Duplicate) — a duplicate is a normal
89	// outcome for an at-least-once producer retrying, not an error. The
90	// stream, sequence, and duplicate outcome are also recorded on the span.
91	func (p Publisher) Publish(ctx context.Context, msg *nats.Msg, msgID string, attrs ...attribute.KeyValue) (*jetstream.PubAck, error) {
92		tr := p.Tracer
93		if tr == nil {
94			tr = otel.Tracer("github.com/entireio/go-nuts/natsmsg")
95		}
96		name := p.Operation
97		if name == "" {
98			name = "publish " + msg.Subject
99		}
100		ctx, span := StartProducerSpan(ctx, tr, msg.Subject, name, attrs...)
101		defer span.End()
102	
103		if msgID != "" {
104			if msg.Header == nil {
105				msg.Header = nats.Header{}
106			}
107			msg.Header.Set(nats.MsgIdHdr, msgID)
108			span.SetAttributes(attribute.String("messaging.message.id", msgID))
109		}
110		Inject(ctx, msg)
111	
112		timeout := p.Timeout
113		if timeout == 0 {
114			timeout = DefaultPublishTimeout
115		}
116		pubCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, timeout)
117		defer cancel()
118	
119		ack, err := p.JS.PublishMsg(pubCtx, msg)
120		if err != nil {
121			span.RecordError(err)
122			span.SetStatus(codes.Error, "publish")
123			return nil, fmt.Errorf("natsmsg: publish %s: %w", msg.Subject, err)
124		}
125		span.SetAttributes(
126			attribute.String("messaging.nats.stream", ack.Stream),
127			attribute.Int64("messaging.nats.sequence", ClampToInt64(ack.Sequence)),
128			attribute.Bool("messaging.nats.duplicate", ack.Duplicate),
129		)
130		return ack, nil
131	}

2	// NATS consumers handle. It lives apart from the packages under test so
3	// white-box unit tests (package foo, not foo_test) can import it without
4	// cycles or extra fixture dependencies.

7	import (
8		"context"
9		"errors"
10		"time"
11	
12		"github.com/nats-io/nats.go"
13		"github.com/nats-io/nats.go/jetstream"

16	// FakeMsg is a jetstream.Msg for unit-testing a consumer's message disposition
17	// without a live broker. Script the fields the handler reads (SubjectVal,
18	// DataVal, HeadersVal, Meta) and assert the terminal call it made (Acked,
19	// Termed, Naks, NakDelays). Because jetstream.Msg is an interface — unlike the
20	// concrete *nats.Msg whose Ack/Nak/Term hit the wire — the disposition is
21	// directly observable. Script NakErr / TermErr to exercise a caller's
22	// disposition-error path.
23	type FakeMsg struct {
24		SubjectVal string
25		DataVal    []byte
26		HeadersVal nats.Header
27		Meta       *jetstream.MsgMetadata
28		MetaErr    error
29		NakErr     error // returned by Nak/NakWithDelay after the call is recorded
30		TermErr    error // returned by Term/TermWithReason after the call is recorded
31	
32		Acked       bool
33		Termed      bool
34		Naks        int // plain Nak() calls; delayed naks land in NakDelays
35		NakDelays   []time.Duration
36		InProgressN int
37	}
38	
39	func (m *FakeMsg) Subject() string      { return m.SubjectVal }
40	func (m *FakeMsg) Data() []byte         { return m.DataVal }
41	func (m *FakeMsg) Headers() nats.Header { return m.HeadersVal }
42	func (m *FakeMsg) Reply() string        { return "" }
43	
44	// Metadata returns the scripted metadata, the scripted error, or — when neither
45	// is set — a non-JetStream error, matching how *nats.Msg.Metadata behaves for a
46	// message that carries none. Consumers guard this with `if err == nil`.
47	func (m *FakeMsg) Metadata() (*jetstream.MsgMetadata, error) {
48		if m.MetaErr != nil {
49			return nil, m.MetaErr
50		}
51		if m.Meta != nil {
52			return m.Meta, nil
53		}
54		return nil, errors.New("fakemsg: no metadata set")
55	}
56	
57	func (m *FakeMsg) Ack() error                      { m.Acked = true; return nil }
58	func (m *FakeMsg) DoubleAck(context.Context) error { m.Acked = true; return nil }
59	func (m *FakeMsg) Nak() error                      { m.Naks++; return m.NakErr }
60	func (m *FakeMsg) NakWithDelay(d time.Duration) error {
61		m.NakDelays = append(m.NakDelays, d)
62		return m.NakErr
63	}
64	func (m *FakeMsg) InProgress() error           { m.InProgressN++; return nil }
65	func (m *FakeMsg) Term() error                 { m.Termed = true; return m.TermErr }
66	func (m *FakeMsg) TermWithReason(string) error { m.Termed = true; return m.TermErr }
67	
68	var _ jetstream.Msg = (*FakeMsg)(nil)

# go-nuts A small, dependency-light toolkit over [`nats.go`](https://github.com/nats-io/nats.go) for building [NATS](https://nats.io) and JetStream services in Go. The root package handles connection lifecycle — connecting, draining, and shutting down cleanly; opt-in subpackages add a durable JetStream pull-consumer scaffold, a publish helper, trace-context propagation, and a redelivery policy. ## Install ``` go get github.com/entireio/go-nuts ``` ## Connection lifecycle (root package) - **`Connect`** — dial with a resilient default posture: reconnect-forever (so a long-lived service rides out a NATS outage instead of permanently closing after the client's default 60 attempts), a bounded drain timeout, optional rotation-aware mTLS, and lifecycle log handlers that don't mistake a clean shutdown for a fault. Async errors (slow-consumer drops, permissions violations) and lame-duck notices are logged through the configured logger instead of nats.go's stderr default. - **`Drain` / `IsShutdownFetchErr`** — graceful shutdown. `Drain` starts nats.go's asynchronous drain and blocks until the connection flushes and closes (bounded by a timeout), returning an error and force-closing when it cannot complete; `IsShutdownFetchErr` lets a fetch loop treat a drain/close during shutdown as a clean exit rather than an error. - **`ShutdownGroup`** — cancels tracked background loops, waits for them to return, then drains the registered connections — the ordering that keeps a `Drain` from racing an in-flight `Fetch`. A panic or unexpected return in a tracked loop cancels the group and is returned by `Shutdown`, so a dead consumer cannot leave its process looking healthy. ## Usage The example below drives a hand-rolled fetch loop on nats.go's legacy pull API; consumers on the modern `jetstream` API get the whole loop from [`jsconsumer`](#subpackages) instead. ```go ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM) defer stop() g := nuts.NewShutdownGroup(ctx) nc, err := nuts.Connect(g.Context(), natsURL, nuts.WithName("worker")) if err != nil { return err } g.AddConn("worker", nc) g.Go(func(ctx context.Context) { for { // Stop fetching once the group is shutting down, so the loop returns // before its connection is drained (Shutdown cancels, joins, then // drains — the loop must observe the cancel to keep that ordering). if ctx.Err() != nil { return } msgs, err := sub.Fetch(1, nats.MaxWait(5*time.Second)) switch { case errors.Is(err, nats.ErrTimeout): continue // idle poll case nuts.IsShutdownFetchErr(ctx, err): return // clean shutdown: connection drained/closed case err != nil: // Real error — log/metric, then back off so a fast-failing Fetch // (e.g. connection closed mid-run) does not busy-spin the CPU. slog.ErrorContext(ctx, "fetch failed", slog.Any("error", err)) select { case <-ctx.Done(): case <-time.After(time.Second): } continue } handle(msgs) } }) <-g.Context().Done() // process signal, or a tracked loop failed if err := g.Shutdown(); err != nil { // cancel loops → join → drain, in that order return err } ``` By default `Connect` builds mTLS from the `ENTIRE_INTERNAL_TLS_{CERT,KEY,CA}_FILE` environment variables; use `WithTLSConfig`, `WithoutTLS`, or the other `Option`s to override. ## Subpackages The root package is deliberately nats.go-only. The consumer-side layers live in subpackages so importing the root links none of their dependencies (`natsmsg` and `jsconsumer` add the OpenTelemetry API; all three use `nats.go/jetstream`): - **`natsmsg`** — small JetStream message helpers: W3C trace-context propagation over message headers (`Inject` / `ExtractHeader` / `StartConsumerSpan`, so publish → consume stitches into one trace), `Publisher` — the publish core (producer span with a caller-selected `Operation` name + standard `messaging.*` attributes + trace inject + `Nats-Msg-Id` dedup + bounded pub-ack wait + PubAck telemetry, with `StartProducerSpan` for callers composing by hand); it owns just that prologue — subject construction, payload encoding, domain metrics/logging, and the response to a failed publish stay with the caller (its `JS` field is the narrow publish slice of `jetstream.JetStream`, so tests stub one method). Also `KeepInProgress`, an AckWait heartbeat for long handlers, capped so a wedged handler still redelivers, and `DeadLetter` / `SubjectToken`, the dead-letter capture that copies a poison message to a DLQ subject with `Nats-Dlq-*` provenance before a consumer gives up on it (the capture step `backoff`'s Term-on-exhaustion below expects). `natsmsg/natsmsgtest` ships `FakeMsg`, a scriptable message for asserting a consumer's ack/nak/term disposition without a broker. - **`jsconsumer`** — the durable JetStream pull-consumer scaffold: `Start` (create-or-update durable → consume → stop on context cancel), `Run` (`Start` under supervision: recreate on a closed loop with exponential backoff, tolerate a not-yet-provisioned stream at boot), and `Process` (consumer span re-parented across the NATS hop → decode → Term-on-undecodable → dispatch to the handler, which owns the message's disposition). AckExplicit, bounded AckWait and MaxDeliver, optional InactiveThreshold / MaxAckPending, shutdown-aware consume-error logging, optional `KeepInProgress` heartbeat. - **`backoff`** — the redelivery policy for transiently-failed deliveries: a `NakWithDelay` envelope — flat by default, optionally growing per delivery (`Factor`/`MaxDelay`) — bounded by MaxDeliver, with opt-in Term-on-final-delivery so a work-queue message is removed cleanly instead of orphaning un-acked. It owns disposition and delay calculation only (`NakOrTerm` over `jetstream.Msg`). MaxDeliver mirrors `jetstream.ConsumerConfig`: a non-positive value (`0` or `UnlimitedMaxDeliver`) means unlimited redeliveries, so bridge an unset `jsconsumer` consumer with its `EffectiveMaxDeliver()` rather than the raw field. ## Development Requires Go 1.26. Tasks via [mise](https://mise.jdx.dev): `mise run test`, `mise run lint`, `mise run fmt`. ## License MIT — see [LICENSE](./LICENSE).

Also `KeepInProgress`, an AckWait heartbeat for long handlers, capped so a wedged handler still redelivers, and `DeadLetter` / `SubjectToken`, the dead-letter capture that copies a poison message to a DLQ subject with `Nats-Dlq-*` provenance before a consumer gives up on it (the capture step `backoff`'s Term-on-exhaustion below expects). `natsmsg/natsmsgtest` ships `FakeMsg`, a scriptable message for asserting a consumer's ack/nak/term disposition without a broker. - **`jsconsumer`** — the durable JetStream pull-consumer scaffold: `Start` (create-or-update durable → consume → stop on context cancel), `Run` (`Start` under supervision: recreate on a closed loop with exponential backoff, tolerate a not-yet-provisioned stream at boot), and `Process` (consumer span re-parented across the NATS hop → decode → Term-on-undecodable → dispatch to the handler, which owns the message's disposition). AckExplicit, bounded AckWait and MaxDeliver, optional InactiveThreshold / MaxAckPending, shutdown-aware consume-error logging, optional `KeepInProgress` heartbeat. - **`backoff`** — the redelivery policy for transiently-failed deliveries: a `NakWithDelay` envelope — flat by default, optionally growing per delivery (`Factor`/`MaxDelay`) — bounded by MaxDeliver, with opt-in Term-on-final-delivery so a work-queue message is removed cleanly instead of orphaning un-acked. It owns disposition and delay calculation only (`NakOrTerm` over `jetstream.Msg`). MaxDeliver mirrors `jetstream.ConsumerConfig`: a non-positive value (`0` or `UnlimitedMaxDeliver`) means unlimited redeliveries, so bridge an unset `jsconsumer` consumer with its `EffectiveMaxDeliver()` rather than the raw field. ## Development Requires Go 1.26. Tasks via [mise](https://mise.jdx.dev): `mise run test`, `mise run lint`, `mise run fmt`. ## License MIT — see [LICENSE](./LICENSE).

- **`jsconsumer.Retry`** — the consumer's *single* retry mechanism: one
  redelivery ladder, a **floor-age circuit breaker**, and the dead-letter
  capture both terminate into. A JetStream consumer has two redelivery
  schedulers — the server's `ConsumerConfig.BackOff` and the handler's own
  `NakWithDelay` — and setting both does not pick one: the server stretches
  each NAK delay by the BackOff increments, so the configured ladder becomes
  dead config that still reads as authoritative (ENT-1535 measured a real
  34h22m envelope against a documented 17h45m). `Config.BackOff` and
  `Config.Retry` are therefore mutually exclusive — a `Start` error — and
  adopting a `Retry` clears any ladder already on the durable.

  The breaker triggers on **floor-stationary age**, not message stream-age:

toolUseResult.originalFile: # go-nuts A small, dependency-light toolkit over [`nats.go`](https://github.com/nats-io/nats.go) for building [NATS](https://nats.io) and JetStream services in Go. The root package handles connection lifecycle — connecting, draining, and shutting down cleanly; opt-in subpackages add a durable JetStream pull-consumer scaffold, a publish helper, trace-context propagation, and a redelivery policy. ## Install ``` go get github.com/entireio/go-nuts ``` ## Connection lifecycle (root package) - **`Connect`** — dial with a resilient default posture: reconnect-forever (so a long-lived service rides out a NATS outage instead of permanently closing after the client's default 60 attempts), a bounded drain timeout, optional rotation-aware mTLS, and lifecycle log handlers that don't mistake a clean shutdown for a fault. Async errors (slow-consumer drops, permissions violations) and lame-duck notices are logged through the configured logger instead of nats.go's stderr default. - **`Drain` / `IsShutdownFetchErr`** — graceful shutdown. `Drain` starts nats.go's asynchronous drain and blocks until the connection flushes and closes (bounded by a timeout), returning an error and force-closing when it cannot complete; `IsShutdownFetchErr` lets a fetch loop treat a drain/close during shutdown as a clean exit rather than an error. - **`ShutdownGroup`** — cancels tracked background loops, waits for them to return, then drains the registered connections — the ordering that keeps a `Drain` from racing an in-flight `Fetch`. A panic or unexpected return in a tracked loop cancels the group and is returned by `Shutdown`, so a dead consumer cannot leave its process looking healthy. ## Usage The example below drives a hand-rolled fetch loop on nats.go's legacy pull API; consumers on the modern `jetstream` API get the whole loop from [`jsconsumer`](#subpackages) instead. ```go ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM) defer stop() g := nuts.NewShutdownGroup(ctx) nc, err := nuts.Connect(g.Context(), natsURL, nuts.WithName("worker")) if err != nil { return err } g.AddConn("worker", nc) g.Go(func(ctx context.Context) { for { // Stop fetching once the group is shutting down, so the loop returns // before its connection is drained (Shutdown cancels, joins, then // drains — the loop must observe the cancel to keep that ordering). if ctx.Err() != nil { return } msgs, err := sub.Fetch(1, nats.MaxWait(5*time.Second)) switch { case errors.Is(err, nats.ErrTimeout): continue // idle poll case nuts.IsShutdownFetchErr(ctx, err): return // clean shutdown: connection drained/closed case err != nil: // Real error — log/metric, then back off so a fast-failing Fetch // (e.g. connection closed mid-run) does not busy-spin the CPU. slog.ErrorContext(ctx, "fetch failed", slog.Any("error", err)) select { case <-ctx.Done(): case <-time.After(time.Second): } continue } handle(msgs) } }) <-g.Context().Done() // process signal, or a tracked loop failed if err := g.Shutdown(); err != nil { // cancel loops → join → drain, in that order return err } ``` By default `Connect` builds mTLS from the `ENTIRE_INTERNAL_TLS_{CERT,KEY,CA}_FILE` environment variables; use `WithTLSConfig`, `WithoutTLS`, or the other `Option`s to override. ## Subpackages The root package is deliberately nats.go-only. The consumer-side layers live in subpackages so importing the root links none of their dependencies (`natsmsg` and `jsconsumer` add the OpenTelemetry API; all three use `nats.go/jetstream`): - **`natsmsg`** — small JetStream message helpers: W3C trace-context propagation over message headers (`Inject` / `ExtractHeader` / `StartConsumerSpan`, so publish → consume stitches into one trace), `Publisher` — the publish core (producer span with a caller-selected `Operation` name + standard `messaging.*` attributes + trace inject + `Nats-Msg-Id` dedup + bounded pub-ack wait + PubAck telemetry, with `StartProducerSpan` for callers composing by hand); it owns just that prologue — subject construction, payload encoding, domain metrics/logging, and the response to a failed publish stay with the caller (its `JS` field is the narrow publish slice of `jetstream.JetStream`, so tests stub one method). Also `KeepInProgress`, an AckWait heartbeat for long handlers, capped so a wedged handler still redelivers, and `DeadLetter` / `SubjectToken`, the dead-letter capture that copies a poison message to a DLQ subject with `Nats-Dlq-*` provenance before a consumer gives up on it (the capture step `backoff`'s Term-on-exhaustion below expects). `natsmsg/natsmsgtest` ships `FakeMsg`, a scriptable message for asserting a consumer's ack/nak/term disposition without a broker. - **`jsconsumer`** — the durable JetStream pull-consumer scaffold: `Start` (create-or-update durable → consume → stop on context cancel), `Run` (`Start` under supervision: recreate on a closed loop with exponential backoff, tolerate a not-yet-provisioned stream at boot), and `Process` (consumer span re-parented across the NATS hop → decode → Term-on-undecodable → dispatch to the handler, which owns the message's disposition). AckExplicit, bounded AckWait and MaxDeliver, optional InactiveThreshold / MaxAckPending, shutdown-aware consume-error logging, optional `KeepInProgress` heartbeat. - **`backoff`** — the redelivery policy for transiently-failed deliveries: a `NakWithDelay` envelope — flat by default, optionally growing per delivery (`Factor`/`MaxDelay`) — bounded by MaxDeliver, with opt-in Term-on-final-delivery so a work-queue message is removed cleanly instead of orphaning un-acked. It owns disposition and delay calculation only (`NakOrTerm` over `jetstream.Msg`). MaxDeliver mirrors `jetstream.ConsumerConfig`: a non-positive value (`0` or `UnlimitedMaxDeliver`) means unlimited redeliveries, so bridge an unset `jsconsumer` consumer with its `EffectiveMaxDeliver()` rather than the raw field. ## Development Requires Go 1.26. Tasks via [mise](https://mise.jdx.dev): `mise run test`, `mise run lint`, `mise run fmt`. ## License MIT — see [LICENSE](./LICENSE).
